title: Bollywood’s Screenwriters Are Begging for Love Stories — But Producers Only Want Blood
excerpt: Horror dominates, franchises feast on nostalgia, and the writers who create Bollywood’s soul say the industry has lost the conviction to try anything new
body:
The first half of 2026 is over, and Bollywood's numbers look sensational. Three thousand crore at the domestic box office. A revenge saga called *Dhurandhar: The Revenge* that crossed ₹1,800 crore globally and rewrote the commercial playbook. **Akshay Kumar** landed a horror-comedy hit with *Bhooth Bangla*. **Sunny Deol** made everyone cry with *Border 2*. **Imtiaz Ali** proved slow-burn still works with *Main Vaapas Aaunga*, the little film that opened to empty halls and now can't print tickets fast enough.

But behind the celebrations, in the rooms where scripts are pitched and dreams are sold, something feels off.

In a revealing new report from *The Hollywood Reporter India*, five of the industry's most respected screenwriters — including **Alankrita Shrivastava** (*Made in Heaven*, *Lipstick Under My Burkha*), **Saiwyn Quadras** (*Neerja*, *Maidaan*), and **Charudutt Acharya**, president of the Screenwriters Association — describe an industry running on imitation, not imagination. The picture they paint is far less glamorous than the red-carpet version Bollywood sells.

The consensus? Producers want horror. Specifically, the kind that *Bhooth Bangla* delivered — mid-budget, high-return, familiar enough to fill seats. The global success of *Obsession*, the $750K American indie that crossed $371 million worldwide, has only accelerated the feeding frenzy. Every producer in Bandra now wants a "clever horror" script on their desk by Monday morning.

> "Post *Dhurandhar*, producers I have met seem unsure about what to take a punt on. The only trend I see is confusion and lack of conviction." — Saiwyn Quadras

The irony is that nobody disagrees about what's actually missing. Across every interview, every single writer named the same orphaned genre: **romance**. The sweeping, cinematic, grown-up love story that Bollywood once owned like no other industry on earth.

**Ankur Pathak** (*Modern Love Mumbai*, *Family Business*) put it bluntly: rom-coms and romantic dramas are "our core storytelling strength, and we've almost forgotten how to make them." He described an industry that has replaced love stories with narratives "fetishising war and rewarding violence," while "a disturbing element of crude machismo has crept into mainstream storytelling." He wants someone to make another *Dil Chahta Hai*, another *Wake Up Sid* — the kind of film that captures a generation's mood without needing a ₹300-crore VFX budget to justify its existence.

Shrivastava was sharper still: "Nobody seems to want a quiet, gentle piece of storytelling right now." She praised the few bright spots on streaming — women-led series like *Maa Behen* and *Chiraiya* that challenge patriarchy from the margins — while noting that the big screen has all but abandoned the intimate, personal film. "I think this is the time to take risks," she said, pointing to the success of *Obsession* as proof that genre filmmaking with real ideas can still find massive audiences.

For NRIs scrolling through streaming catalogues thousands of miles from home, this creative drought has a tangible cost. The slice-of-life Indian stories that once connected diaspora audiences to the texture of home — the feeling of a Mumbai monsoon, the chaos of a family dinner, the ache of leaving — have all but vanished from theatrical slates. In their place: franchise sequels, franchise prequels, and franchise spinoffs, each algorithmically optimised to look exactly like the last thing that worked.

And the streaming platforms aren't helping. Pathak described a system where "algorithmic success has replaced the box-office yardstick." When a crime-thriller lands on a streamer, it becomes the template for everything that follows — wounded cops, spooky North Indian towns, corruption sagas with a messianic hero. "Our collective imaginations rarely permit us to be more adventurous," he said.

The second half of 2026 promises more of what the first half delivered — big, expensive, star-powered tentpoles. **Alia Bhatt**'s *Alpha* arrives Thursday as the first female-led chapter of the YRF Spy Universe. *Dhamaal 4* follows on July 10 with Bollywood's maddest franchise circus. **Ranbir Kapoor**'s *Ramayana* and **Shah Rukh Khan**'s *King* loom further out like approaching weather systems. All of them will probably make money. Some will be genuinely spectacular.

But the writers who build these worlds are warning that the engine is running on fumes.

**Satyanshu Singh** (*Black Warrant*, *Chintu Ka Birthday*) offered the most sobering advice: if you start writing to match today's trends, by the time the film is made, that trend will be dead and the market will be flooded with bad copies. "Instead of looking outwards, we should look inwards. You can't design your scripts based on trends — that never works out."

The SWA, meanwhile, is pushing for systemic change: basic minimum contracts and royalty collection for writers, measures that would give screenwriters the financial security to take creative risks rather than chase commissions. Whether the industry listens is another matter entirely.

Bollywood's ticket sales are robust. Its creative conviction is not. And if the industry keeps telling its best storytellers to bring horror scripts or nothing at all, it might wake up one morning to find that the love story it forgot to tell was its own.
